Yes. We already did that audit, and it was fairly useful.



The prior **LEGACYCHAT-FEED-RANKING-AUDIT001** looked at both the available ranking signals **and the query/index cost of using them**. Its main conclusions were:



- We already have usable fields for topic/post time, reply counts, zero-reply state, board/group identity, memberships, recent-board activity, views, likes, media, and some read/unread state.

- Membership lookup was already well-supported by an index on `tnet_memberships(user_id, group_id)`.

- The existing feed had a real **N+1** pattern: one `tnet_groups` lookup per distinct board in the returned feed.

- Deep offset pagination was not ideal for eventual infinite/progressive loading; the audit favored a stable cursor/keyset approach.

- Global ranking across the entire archive would be unnecessarily expensive. The recommended model was **bounded candidate selection → bulk enrichment → scoring**.

- Raw lifetime views/likes were poor primary ranking inputs because they can over-favor old content and require less attractive aggregation patterns.

- The audit specifically called for reviewing query plans and indexes before adding new indexes rather than blindly indexing everything.



And the ticket we just ran gave us another useful performance clue: Codex initially tried a **join-heavy query for the single proof card and it exceeded the browser navigation timeout**. It then replaced that with a bounded root-row query plus narrow keyed lookups, bringing the local page back to about **0.64 seconds**. 



So we already know the broad strategy:



> **Avoid giant joins over the legacy dataset. Pull a bounded candidate set using indexed fields, then enrich those candidates in bulk/keyed lookups.**



What we have **not yet done** is a final implementation-specific performance audit of the exact `/newskin/` feed query after all the new components/ranking logic are assembled. That will be worth doing before we put infinite scroll on top of it or deploy it to a high-traffic page.

The official Adobe XD sharing model supports viewing shared prototypes, grid navigation, comments, and—in **Development** shares—downloadable assets when the designer explicitly marks them for export. There is, however, an older Adobe XD **Cloud Content API** documented for published links. It exposes discovery plus document/artboard endpoints, including `/v2/api`, `/v2/document/{linkID}`, and `/v2/document/{linkID}/artboard/{artboardID}`. The discovery call takes the published XD URL in an `X-AdobeXD-Link` header. ([Adobe XD Platform](https://adobexdplatform.com/cloud-content-api-docs/reference/))



So I see three possible adapters:



- **Browser-capture adapter:** use a real browser session to open the prototype, enumerate artboards/screens, and capture them as images/PDF. This is the most likely to work for your existing public view link.

This may require an Adobe API key/authentication and may be legacy/partially retired, so it needs experimentation. ([Adobe XD Platform](https://adobexdplatform.com/cloud-content-api-docs/reference/))

- **Development-spec adapter:** if whoever owns the XD file can republish it as a Development share with downloadable assets, Adobe officially supports asset extraction/download from that view. ([Adobe Help Center](https://helpx-origin-ew1.aws116.adobeitc.com/se/xd/desktop/share-export-and-review/extract-assets-from-design-specs.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))



I would **not use third-party “XD downloader” sites** for this. A view-only share is intentionally not a source-file download mechanism, and those services tend to be unreliable or credential-harvesting risks.



For our actual goal—**inspect this presentation so we can learn from its UI/design**—we don't need the `.xd` source file. The best target is probably a small adapter that:

## The biggest archaeological finding



This wasn't merely a redesign.



You had already conceived a fairly complete **Teachers.Net social/community operating model**:



**Identity → interests/groups → personalized home → discussion → engagement → notifications → relationships → messaging → content/resources/jobs.**



A striking amount of what we've independently been deriving for Community 3.0 is already represented here.



That doesn't mean we should resurrect this design. In many respects our current architecture is substantially better. But it means this is valuable **product-intent evidence**.



### RECOVER / make sure 3.0 explicitly covers



The strongest finds are:



- **Real notifications.** Screen 034 is almost a specification for the problem we recently identified: bell count → dropdown → explicit events → unread state → timestamps → mark-read → settings. Plus toast notification.

- **Reply notifications at creation time.** The expanded topic composer explicitly offers “Send me post reply notifications.” That's an extremely sensible return loop.

- **Inline reply-to-comment.** The thread view gives replies their own Reply/Like controls. We've already identified this as a major omission in today's live system.

- **New activity indicators.** Some discussion cards distinguish new comments/activity rather than merely showing total comments.

- **My Groups versus All Groups.** Excellent conceptual split between personalization and discovery.

- **Activity history.** Profile activity isn't decorative—it gives users a route back to things they've done.

- **Messaging.** Not interim scope, but 040 demonstrates that direct/group messaging was part of the intended community machine, not an unrelated idea.

- **Public relationship state.** Follow/friend/request/message concepts exist. We needn't adopt Facebook-style “friends,” but Community 3.0 needs an explicit decision about relationships rather than accidentally omitting the question.

- **Group-local ecosystems.** A group isn't merely a filter on discussions: designs contemplate Discussions, Blogs, Lessons, Gallery, Jobs and Members within a community context.

- **Cross-product contextualization.** That's potentially important. A Science Teachers community could eventually surface science jobs, lessons, discussions and resources without those products becoming one monolith.



## ALREADY COVERED — often better now



Several old ideas have essentially evolved into stronger current architecture.



### Groups taxonomy → Core Terms + Views + subscriptions



The old:



> State / Grade / Subject / Reading-Writing / Miscellaneous Groups



was a useful product model, but our current work has separated concepts much better.



Today we understand:



**Core Terms → Views → consumer-specific subsets → subscriptions**



rather than making “group category” simultaneously own taxonomy, UI and application semantics.



That's a major architectural improvement.



### Group membership as personalization



The old designs repeatedly use membership to determine:



- what appears in navigation;

- what appears in feeds;

- membership stars/checks;

- activity;

- discovery.



We're doing the same conceptually, but now membership can coexist with Views and other interest signals.



### Compact composer



Screens 028/029 and 032/033 are almost uncanny given our recent discussion.



You had already landed on:



> tiny composer → activate → substantial creation interface.



Our current `/newskin/` implementation is a cleaner modern expression of essentially the same idea.



### Three-column community shell



Again, repeated convergence.



Old:



> persistent left navigation | central feed | right discovery/advertising



Current:



> persistent utility rail | 728px primary feed | 300px monetization/support rail.



The new design is more disciplined about widths, responsive collapse and advertising requirements.



## INVESTIGATE



There are several concepts I wouldn't automatically adopt, but I would explicitly put them on the 3.0 decision checklist.



**Relationships:** Follow? Friends? Both? Neither? Teacher-to-teacher connections have product value, but we need a deliberate relationship model.



**Group-local resources:** Should a Chatboard/community eventually aggregate Jobs, Lessons and other resources matching its Terms? The old mock strongly suggests yes, and our current Views architecture makes this much more feasible.



**Activity/profile history:** How much user activity is public versus private? Very useful, but now we would design privacy deliberately.



**Likes as signals:** The old design assumes likes have consequences—they generate notifications and appear in activity. That's exactly why our current meaningless Like feels weak. If we retain Like, it should participate in the system.



**Group discovery:** The one-click join/leave catalog is still appealing. Views could make a much better version of this.



**“Popular Now”:** The right rail repeatedly uses this. Our modern equivalent might be Trending/Active Around Teachers.Net, but the underlying discovery function remains valid.



## SUPERSEDED



Some old concepts have aged poorly.



The giant collection of user-selectable color themes is interesting archaeology but not something I'd resurrect. **Light/dark/system** is probably enough unless personalization becomes a strategic feature.



The Facebook-era **Friends** model probably shouldn't simply be copied.



The icon-only global navbar is visually clean but ambiguous. Our current nav discussion is better grounded in actual product destinations.



Some profile statistics—raw counts of friends/groups/posts/blogs—feel more like early-social-network status furniture than useful teacher experience.



And the very narrow central columns in several screens would be a regression from the 728px center we've now established.



## DISCARD / SCRAP



The later chrome permutations—different left-navigation hierarchies, swapping Home/Groups emphasis, multiple near-identical Science/Connecticut layouts—should not be interpreted as competing requirements.



They're useful because they demonstrate that you were experimenting with:



- global vs contextual navigation;

- group context in the left rail;

- active global-product state;

- whether group subnavigation belongs horizontally or vertically.



But they're sketches, not authority.



---

**Contextual transformation of the shell.**



Look at what happens when the user enters *Science Teachers*.



The overall Teachers.Net application doesn't disappear, but parts of the shell become contextual:



> Science Teachers  

> Discussions  

> Blogs  

> Lessons  

> Gallery  

> Jobs  

> Members



That's a sophisticated idea.



With our current architecture, imagine entering **Elementary Teachers** and having contextual access to:



- Discussions

- Jobs

- Lessons

- perhaps Projects/resources



all resolved through shared Terms/Views.



That's much more powerful now than it would have been when these mocks were made because we've actually developed the classification architecture capable of supporting it.



I would classify that as **DEFER TO 3.0, HIGH-VALUE**.



## And the most important validation



Our current `/newskin/` direction does **not** look like we're wandering away from the old product vision.



Quite the opposite.



We're reconstructing its strongest ideas with:



- better information architecture;

- cleaner data ownership;

- explicit taxonomy;

- responsive strategy;

- modern feed conventions;

- performance discipline;

- better advertising geometry;

- isolation between products;

- an actual migration strategy.



So I would **not change course on `/newskin/` because of this dig**.



I would use the dig to create a **Community 3.0 completeness checklist** so that when we eventually say “3.0 architecture is complete,” we're certain we consciously addressed notifications, relationships, messaging, activity, contextual communities, resource integration, personalization, discovery, privacy, and engagement loops.



The excavation has mostly validated our direction—but it has also recovered several valuable pieces we could easily have forgotten.

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-000510-U — USER

what did we find out?

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-000511-A — ASSISTANT

We learned something important: **the N+1 problem is real, but it is not the main performance problem. The root-topic selection query is.**



## 1. The current full-feed shape would be unacceptable



Our single-card data seam uses **6 SQL statements**.



Naively repeating that for 20 cards becomes **101 statements**: one candidate query plus roughly five enrichment queries per card, with another per-card query possible for authenticated Like state. 



Codex proved the fix we expected:



| 20-card retrieval | Queries | Cold-ish DB | Warm DB |

|---|---:|---:|---:|

| Current repeated shape | **101** | 570 ms | 262 ms |

| Bulk-enriched shape | **6** | 351 ms | 222 ms |



So we can eliminate essentially the entire SQL N+1 explosion: fetch the candidate roots once, then batch local/group mappings, memberships, replies and likes. 



That's excellent architecturally.



## 2. But candidate selection is surprisingly expensive



This is the bigger finding.



The database has about **172,000 chatposts**, of which roughly **58,000 are active root posts**. 



Our current candidate query is basically:



> active root posts → order by `post_datetime DESC, post_id DESC` → LIMIT



And MySQL doesn't have an index that simultaneously supports those fixed predicates **and** that ordering.



The result is:



- `index_merge`

- approximately **40,013 rows examined**

- `Using filesort`



just to choose the newest candidate(s). 



That's why even asking for **one card** produced:



- ~1.03 seconds cold-ish

- ~206 ms warm



with essentially all of that time coming from candidate selection. 



And in the optimized 20-card simulation, candidate selection alone was:



- **338 ms cold**

- **220 ms warm**



while all the bulk enrichment around it was comparatively cheap. 



So our earlier concern about that ~0.64-second page was justified.



## 3. The supporting data structures are actually pretty healthy



This is reassuring.



Codex found useful indexes already supporting:



- local-data lookup;

- group lookup;

- reply counts;

- Like counts;

- current-user Like state;

- membership counts/existence. 



Media also doesn't require another query, and avatars are filesystem resolution rather than SQL. 



So this isn't evidence that the whole legacy database is a disaster.



We have **two specific defects**:



1. per-card enrichment needs batching;

2. root candidate selection needs a better access path.



That's quite manageable.



## 4. There's a very plausible index fix



Codex proposes evaluating something approximately like:



`(status, post_type, post_datetime, post_id)`



That aligns directly with:



> WHERE fixed status/type → ORDER BY datetime/id



and could potentially turn today's index-merge + 40k-row/filesort operation into a very inexpensive ordered index read. 



Importantly, Codex **did not create the index**. That's correct—we asked for diagnosis, not schema mutation.



I'd expect this to be potentially a very high-value index, but we should prove its plan and measured effect rather than assume.



## 5. We also have the pagination architecture



Our deterministic order already gives us the right basis:



`post_datetime DESC, post_id DESC`



So eventual progressive/infinite loading should use a cursor containing:



`(post_datetime, post_id)`



and a seek predicate rather than increasingly expensive `OFFSET`s. 



That's exactly what we wanted to know before building endless scroll.



---



# What I recommend next



I would slightly improve on Codex's recommended next ticket.



It recommends implementing the bounded/bulk retrieval architecture immediately. 



I think we should first **prove the candidate-index hypothesis**, because candidate selection currently dominates everything else.



This is a perfect case for a very narrow performance implementation experiment:



1. establish current candidate-query plan/timing;

2. add the proposed composite index **locally only**;

3. rerun `EXPLAIN` and identical timings;

4. determine whether the filesort/index-merge disappears;

5. measure the actual improvement;

6. inspect index overlap/cost;

7. retain the index only if the evidence is compelling.



Then, assuming it works, the following implementation can combine:



> indexed bounded candidate selection → six-ish bulk enrichment queries → canonical card assembly.



At that point we should have a feed data path I would be comfortable multiplying.



**REASONING: NORMAL remains appropriate.** The diagnostic found one clear owner and a testable index hypothesis; no need to spend MEDIUM yet. 



And our visual note remains queued: on the next visual/product implementation cycle, remove the leaderboard-proof label so the 728×90 fixture can sit flush beneath the navbar.

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-000515-A — ASSISTANT

Very good news, with one wrinkle: **the index hypothesis was spectacularly correct, but MariaDB's optimizer refuses to choose it automatically.**



## Result



Baseline candidate selection was roughly:



- LIMIT 1: **233 ms**

- LIMIT 10: **240 ms**

- LIMIT 20: **234 ms**



The optimizer was doing the bad plan we identified: `index_merge` across existing indexes, examining roughly 35–40K rows, then `filesort`. 



Codex then created our proposed local-only index:



`(status, post_type, post_datetime, post_id)`



When Codex explicitly forced MariaDB to use it, performance became:



| Candidates | Existing plan | New index forced | Reduction |

|---|---:|---:|---:|

| 1 | ~233 ms | **0.336 ms** | ~99.9% |

| 10 | ~240 ms | **0.758 ms** | ~99.7% |

| 20 | ~234 ms | **1.178 ms** | ~99.5% |



That isn't noise. It's roughly a **200–700× improvement**, depending on the batch. 



And critically, the good plan eliminates both **index_merge and filesort** while preserving our deterministic `post_datetime DESC, post_id DESC` ordering. 



## The wrinkle



MariaDB still chooses the old terrible plan **unless we force the new index**.



Even after creating the index and running `ANALYZE TABLE`, unrestricted `EXPLAIN` continued choosing:



> `status + idx_posttype_status` → index merge → filesort



instead of the composite index. 



So we haven't yet proven:



> “Add this index and everything automatically gets 200× faster.”



We've proven:



> **“This index provides an extraordinarily fast access path for exactly our feed query, but this MariaDB optimizer/statistics configuration doesn't recognize that it should use it.”**



That's still an excellent result.



## What it means for our architecture



Our feed performance problem now looks very tractable.



We already established that 20-card enrichment can collapse from **101 queries to about 6** through batching. And now we've demonstrated candidate retrieval itself can fall from ~234 ms to roughly **1 ms for 20 rows**. 



Conceptually, we're heading toward:



**~1ms candidate selection → bounded bulk enrichment → PHP card assembly**



instead of:



**~230ms candidate selection → N×5 enrichment queries → cards**



That is a profound improvement in the prospective hot path.



## One caution



I agree with Codex that we should **not deploy this index to Sandy yet**, much less production.



It overlaps partially with several existing indexes, although none is an exact duplicate. We also need to understand why the optimizer prefers the demonstrably awful plan and whether a narrow `FORCE INDEX`/hint is appropriate for this specific query owner. 



The experimental index remains **local DDEV only**, specifically so the next implementation can exercise the real retrieval path against it. No source or production mutation occurred. 



## Next move



I agree with Codex's proposed next step.



Now implement the actual `/newskin/` data owner as:



**bounded 10–20 candidate selection → bulk/keyed enrichment → existing card assembly**



but **still don't render the full feed**.



During that implementation Codex should compare:



1. normal optimizer selection;

2. narrowly hinted/forced composite-index selection;

3. total assembled 20-topic data cost;

4. identical result/order correctness.



That will tell us whether the final query owner should deliberately select this index.



If we get something resembling **1–2ms candidate selection plus inexpensive bulk enrichment**, we've moved from “performance concern” to a very strong foundation for the real feed.



**NORMAL reasoning remains appropriate.** One owner, one proven fast path, and one unresolved optimizer-selection question.

We settled on **1280px max-width** for the `/newskin/` application shell.



The desktop geometry became:



```text

1280px total

├─ 19px outer allowance

├─ 190px left rail

├─ 12px gutter

├─ 728px center/feed

├─ 12px gutter

├─ 300px right rail

└─ 19px outer allowance

```



The key reason we moved from the earlier **1200px** standard to **1280px** was to preserve both advertising workhorses at native size:



- **728×90 leaderboard** in the center/feed column

- **300×250 medium rectangle** in the right rail



while still retaining a useful left rail.



So for Job Center alignment, the choice we've arrived at is **1280px as the wider Teachers.Net application-shell max-width**. We explicitly left open whether ordinary/content pages should also move from 1200 to 1280, but `/newskin/` established 1280 as the stronger application-shell standard.

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-000531-A — ASSISTANT

The diagnosis is decisive.



## Root cause



The live `/profile/` edit form is being **truncated by a PHP 8.3 fatal error**.



On a normal GET:



1. `profile.php` calls `btr_update_profile()`.

2. Because the request is not POST, that function returns before initializing global `$update_errors`.

3. The template later calls `btr_print_errors($update_errors)`.

4. `btr_print_errors()` does `count($update_errors)`.

5. Under PHP 8.3, `count(null)` throws a `TypeError`.

6. Rendering stops immediately after the hidden nonce/referer/username fields—before the editable fields, Save/Return controls, closing form, and footer. 



So this is **not** a CSS issue, missing BuddyPress fields, AJAX issue, or account-specific defect. It is systemic for the current GET edit path. All expected xProfile field definitions are present. 



## Why the page still looked superficially alive



The response still presents as HTTP 200 because the legacy runtime/error handling doesn't convert the fatal into a useful browser error page. The HTML simply ends early. The authenticated browser response proved exactly that truncation. 



## Source authority is the remaining complication



Codex established the exact active production owner:



`/var/www/htdocs/wp-content/themes/twentysixteen-boss/profile.php`



on Sandy.



The exact same file hash exists locally at:



`~/projects/teachers-net-live/wordpress/wp-content/themes/twentysixteen-boss/profile.php`



But:



- `teachers-net-legacy` does **not** contain `profile.php`;

- no Git lineage was found around the production theme;

- the local copy is currently only a compatibility fixture, not proven durable source authority;

- the newer `tnet-profile` plugin owns avatar-related seams, **not this legacy edit form**. 



That is why Codex did not simply patch production.



## The actual repair is tiny



The report identifies two bounded fixes:



- initialize `$update_errors` to `[]` before the GET path can reach `btr_print_errors()`, or

- make `btr_print_errors()` null-safe.



Either would eliminate this specific PHP 8.3 fatal while preserving the existing edit-field flow. 



I prefer **initializing `$update_errors` as an empty array at its owner**, because that preserves the downstream helper's expectation that it receives an array rather than teaching a generic error printer to compensate for an upstream state bug.



## Recommended next move



We should issue **`PROFILE-EDITPATH-FIX001`**, but its first responsibility should be to establish a durable source/rollback boundary for `profile.php`; then apply only that compatibility fix, verify locally, and deploy through the governed legacy/profile path.



Acceptance should prove:



- authenticated GET renders all expected editable fields;

- no PHP fatal;

- Save works;

- Return works;

- guest redirect remains correct;

- avatar/profile display remains intact;

- no unrelated profile/onboarding behavior changes.



This is a **FAST implementation defect now**, not another diagnostic. The cause and owner are proven.

   - runtime theme/plugin files that are actually live;

   - selected WordPress/config state needed to reproduce routing and behavior.



3. **Local sanitized runtime**

   - `~/projects/teachers-net-live`

   - DDEV

   - production-like code/data/media

   - local URLs/config

   - no production credentials, mail delivery, payment hooks, destructive integrations, etc.



4. **Snapshot manifest**

   - capture date/time;

   - Sandy source hashes;

   - DB dump timestamp;

   - media sync status;

   - exclusions;

   - local transformation steps;

   - missing-source warnings;

   - exact commit(s) represented.



That last piece is essential. Otherwise “local matches production” becomes an assertion we can't verify.



## I would not blindly rsync Sandy



A raw mirror risks copying:



- secrets;

- environment-specific config;

- caches/logs/temp files;

- cron behavior;

- production mail/webhook credentials;

- mutable/generated files that should not become authority.



Instead, build a **bounded refresh workflow**.



Conceptually:



```text

Sandy read-only inventory

        ↓

source/hash comparison

        ↓

database snapshot

        ↓

uploads/media sync

        ↓

approved runtime-only files

        ↓

sanitize/localize config

        ↓

restore into teachers-net-live

        ↓

smoke + parity verification

        ↓

manifest

```



## The most valuable first audit



Before syncing anything, have Codex compare Sandy against `teachers-net-live` and classify every meaningful difference:



- **SOURCE-MANAGED** — already in a governed repo

- **RUNTIME-ONLY** — live file absent from governed source

- **DATA** — database state

- **MEDIA** — uploads/assets

- **ENVIRONMENT** — intentionally different

- **GENERATED/CACHE** — should not sync

- **UNKNOWN** — needs authority decision



That will tell us how far the local runtime has drifted and prevent us from accidentally overwriting newer local/governed work with an old Sandy artifact.



## Refresh cadence



I would make refresh **manual but one-command/repeatable** for now, perhaps eventually:



```bash

./tools/refresh-from-sandy

```



It should default to **read-only on Sandy**, produce a timestamped snapshot, and fail closed on authority contradictions.



For day-to-day work, you could refresh:



- before legacy compatibility work;

- after meaningful Sandy changes;

- whenever Codex reports local/live divergence.



No need for continuous synchronization.



## Database



The DB should be recent enough to reproduce real legacy cases, but restore into a local database only.



I would preserve user/profile/post relationships but sanitize anything sensitive that doesn't need to remain exact. Also disable outbound email and external callbacks locally.



For many bugs, exact production-shaped relational state is more valuable than having perfectly current files.



## Media



For uploads, I'd favor:



- rsync/read-only copy or selective sync of the actual WordPress upload tree;

- preserve paths;

- avoid downloading huge historical media repeatedly if unchanged.



A manifest can record partial media coverage if we choose not to mirror everything.



## My recommendation for the next objective



Before continuing profile repair, I would run a **LOCAL-LIVE-PARITY diagnostic** that answers:



> What is currently missing or divergent between Sandy and `teachers-net-live`, and what exact governed refresh procedure would make the local runtime production-shaped without creating new authority or copying unsafe state?



Then implement the refresh workflow once, rather than fixing missing pieces one by one whenever Codex trips over them.



That should materially reduce future diagnostic cycles across **Profile, Community, and other legacy surfaces**.

Performance diagnostics found two important issues.



The naive 20-card data shape would make **101 SQL queries**. Bulk enrichment reduces the same basic work to about **6 queries**. 



More importantly, candidate selection itself was spending roughly **230ms** because MariaDB used index merging + filesort.

- 1 candidate: **0.336ms**

- 10: **0.758ms**

- 20: **1.178ms**



versus ~230–240ms previously. 



The wrinkle was that MariaDB **wouldn't choose the superior index automatically**.

**`NEWSKIN-FEEDDATA001`**

> 10–20 candidates → bulk enrichment → canonical-card contract



and compare normal optimizer behavior against narrowly hinted use of that index.

Yes—the top card height is an artifact of the render, not something I'd preserve. The **card rhythm should be driven primarily by content density**, not by whether media happens to exist. A compact text post should certainly not become taller than an otherwise comparable media post.



On the post models: I think you're remembering a distinction I made between **three useful feed-card content archetypes**, rather than three different data models:



1. **Standard discussion / text card**  

   The basic case: avatar, board context, title, author/date, excerpt, activity, engagement. “Teacher confused” is the model. This should establish the baseline card rhythm.



2. **Media-enhanced discussion card**  

   Same discussion anatomy, but with attached **image or video** as secondary content. The AI card is the example. On desktop, compact media can occupy the right body region; constrained widths stack it. Video would use the same general region but with appropriate play/state treatment.



3. **Rich/link-preview card**  

   A post containing a URL for which we have structured preview information: destination/site identity, preview title/description and potentially an OG image. This is distinct from a user-attached image because the media represents the **linked resource**, not the post's own attachment. We'd want a compact link-preview treatment rather than pretending it's an uploaded image.



There is potentially a fourth state eventually—**media-led posts** where the image/video itself is essentially the post—but I would *not* introduce that distinction for this interim release unless our existing data clearly tells us that intent. It risks inventing semantics.



### For this design target



I'd design the system around the first three, but keep a **common card skeleton**:



**header/context → title/meta → body payload → engagement**



Only the body payload varies:



- Text → excerpt

- Image/video → excerpt + bounded media

- Link preview → excerpt + compact preview object



And I would explicitly set a **common density/rhythm invariant**: equivalent cards should use the same padding, metadata spacing, engagement baseline, avatar scale, and typography. Media can increase height when it genuinely needs to, but the presence/absence of media shouldn't arbitrarily change the card's basic vertical rhythm.

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-000838-A — ASSISTANT

Yes. I’d separate **2.0 behavior** from **3.0 media architecture** now.



For **Chatcenter 2.0**, I would keep the rule simple: a feed card is primarily a Teachers.Net discussion object. Clicking the card, title, excerpt, avatar context, or engagement should go to the canonical thread. For rich external media, the preview can expose a clearly secondary action like **“Watch on YouTube ↗”**. I would not make the whole card external, and I would not add a Facebook-style modal player in this phase unless we discover it is very cheap. The modal is attractive, but it starts pulling comments, player state, routing, keyboard behavior, mobile behavior, and accessibility into what is supposed to be an interim feed.



For **Community 3.0**, I would aim higher: inline playable video in the feed, with comments/replies available without losing context. That is closer to Facebook’s interaction model and makes sense for a fully evolved community product. But for YouTube/Vimeo-type content, the important point is that **we do not store the video itself**. We store the URL, metadata, thumbnail, provider/video ID, etc.; the provider streams the video. Storage impact is negligible.



The storage concern becomes real only if we allow **direct user video uploads**. Then yes, video gets expensive quickly because you are not just storing one original file. A proper system may need the original plus transcoded renditions, poster/thumbnail images, temporary processing files, potentially captions, and CDN delivery. Even modest uploads can become hundreds of MB per user very quickly.



So I’d lock the roadmap this way:



**2.0:** text posts, attached images if already supported, external rich previews, YouTube-style hosted video links. No direct user video upload requirement.



**3.0:** inline hosted-video playback in feed; richer media posts; potentially direct video uploads only after we deliberately design storage, transcoding, moderation, quotas, CDN, and cost controls.



One additional design point for the target mock: the YouTube preview should look like **supporting media inside a Teachers.Net card**, not like an outbound ad. The card should still read first as:



> “Bob posted this discussion about AI and teaching”



and only secondarily:



> “Here’s the TED video he referenced.”



That will make the feed feel like a community rather than an aggregator.

The key experiment here is the **payload-region grammar**. If Codex can make both attached images and YouTube previews use that right-hand compositional space elegantly, we gain a much stronger common card language:



**text-only card:** content uses available width.  

**payload card:** content voluntarily yields a right-side region to supporting media.



That is one of the reasons the creative mock feels so balanced: the payload affects the composition of the card rather than simply being inserted into it.

Codex also stayed disciplined: the 1280 shell, 190/728/300 columns, real ad dimensions, and responsive owners remained frozen. The changes are presentation-only, and Sandy was untouched. 



### What improved substantially



**The image card is now structurally right.** The robot occupies a genuine 144×104 right-side payload while the title, author and excerpt form a narrower left column.  That's the same compositional trick that makes the aesthetic target work. I would lock this pattern.



**The YouTube side treatment also works conceptually.** I prefer this over the earlier full-width nested preview. It now reads as supporting material belonging to the discussion rather than a second card inserted into it. Codex settled on a 226px payload. 



**The overall page is quieter.** `#f8fafb` is correct. The reduced title size, weaker chrome and lighter engagement treatment all move in the right direction. 



### What still keeps it from feeling like the target



The main remaining difference is **density and vertical rhythm**.



Look at the aesthetic target: cards almost interlock into a continuous conversational stream. In the browser version, each card still feels like a discrete rectangular document with relatively generous vertical space. The YouTube card particularly demonstrates this: its payload is excellent, but the card is **258px tall**, compared with 187px for the image card and 151–169px for text cards. 



I think we can compress that substantially without making it cramped.



The YouTube payload itself is taller than it needs to be. I'd consider making it **wider and shallower** within roughly the same right-side territory—thumbnail on top or left depending on what actually produces the best geometry, but target a card closer to the image-card rhythm. The creative mock's YouTube treatment is much shallower.



### The biggest visual mismatch now: content scale



Interestingly, I don't think 17px titles are the primary problem anymore. The **entire real page feels slightly smaller and more delicate** than the creative target because the fixed 1280 shell contains more whitespace and less visual mass.



The target uses:



- larger avatars;

- stronger board metadata;

- slightly more substantial engagement icons;

- more confident card content;

- more content in the rails.



I would **not enlarge everything globally**. But I would probably restore some visual strength selectively:



- avatars: perhaps 48–50px rather than 46;

- board names: slightly more presence;

- card title 17px is fine;

- engagement icons: a touch stronger;

- body text remains 13px;

- cards get *less* vertical dead space rather than smaller typography.



### The rails



Codex improved them, but the target still handles the left rail better.



The browser rail feels **textual and sparse**. The target uses icons to establish scanning rhythm and has stronger grouping. We deliberately told Codex not to fabricate unsupported features, which was correct, but we can still improve the existing items visually.



I'd add the small icon vocabulary to **Explore** using real destinations we already have. That would give the rail more structure without inventing functionality.



`YOUR TEACHERS.NET` can remain more text-oriented because those are personalized board memberships.



### Right rail



The real right rail is now clean, but almost *too* quiet. The creative target's Continue module has a little more information density: board + recent activity count. Our real implementation just says `Visit`.



If those counts are already cheaply available from existing state, they would be valuable. If not, I wouldn't create a query project merely for aesthetics.



### One thing I actively prefer in Codex's version



The **YouTube payload** is actually conceptually cleaner than the creative mock. It clearly distinguishes:



- Teachers.Net discussion;

- linked YouTube resource;

- explicit outbound action.



So I would use the mock for aesthetic rhythm but **keep Codex's semantic structure**.



### My judgment



We're no longer solving the design system. We're polishing it.



I'd score the progression roughly:



**original live Newskin:** 5/10  

**first precision standard:** 7/10  

**this pass:** **8–8.5/10**



The target remains more visually satisfying, but most of that remaining difference now comes from **rhythm, density, iconography, and a few payload proportions**, not fundamental layout.



I would **not mark final visual PASS yet**, but I also wouldn't issue another broad ticket. One last narrow polish pass should focus on three things:



1. **Compress card vertical rhythm**, especially YouTube.

2. **Give the existing left rail better scanning structure/iconography.**

3. **Tune visual weight inside cards**—avatar/metadata/engagement—without touching the frozen grid or typography architecture.

The best approach is **not to copy the Job Center shell into Community and then reconcile CSS afterward**. We are now far enough along that this should become a **shared-shell convergence objective** with one canonical shell contract and two consumers.



The useful fact is that each side now contributes something valuable:



- **Job Center Shell Lab** already owns the more mature header/footer behavior, dropdowns, responsive collapse, and a deliberately curated variable ecosystem.

- **Newskin** now owns a proven 1280 / 190 / 728 / 300 composition, the 70px header direction, refined feed/content relationship, `#f8fafb` field treatment, card/payload system, and several visual decisions we may want to feed back into the common shell.



So I would not declare either implementation wholesale authority. I would make the **shared shell itself the authority**.



## Recommended architecture



Create a durable **Teachers.Net Shared Shell v1** with four layers:



1. **Shared semantic tokens**  

   Only platform-level variables: navy, primary blue, active blue, muted text, borders, field background, badge red, standard radii, spacing, focus treatment, etc.



2. **Shared shell components**  

   Header, footer, notification/account cluster, dropdown mechanics, desktop alignment, responsive collapse.



3. **Consumer navigation configuration**  

   The shell should not hard-code that every product exposes Jobs, Lessons, Chatboards, etc. Each consumer declares what destinations it can truthfully expose. For Chatcenter 2.0, we can simply omit `Job Center` until there is a useful destination.



4. **Product content region**  

   Job Center retains its application content. Community retains the Newskin 728px feed and rails. The shared shell must not own those product internals.



That distinction is important. We want to reuse **shell behavior and visual language**, not turn Community into a Job Center stylesheet consumer.

- spacing/radius/border standards;

- notification/account treatment;

- footer behavior;

The decisive output should be a proposed **Shared Shell v1 contract**, with explicit dispositions such as:

> membership gold: Community-local semantic

Once we accept the reconciliation, Codex should extract or establish the canonical shared shell owner and migrate **Community first** to consume it.



I would preserve these Newskin seams as acceptance invariants:



> 1280 shell → 190 / 12 / 728 / 12 / 300 / 19 body geometry

> membership system unchanged

Then replace only the shell layer with the canonical shared implementation:



**shared header + dropdowns + notification/account + responsive collapse + footer + shared tokens**

## Then reverse-converge Job Center



After Community passes, we should ensure Job Center itself consumes the same canonical source rather than retaining a private “original” version.

and instead get:



**Shared Shell v1 → Job Center adapter/config**  

**Shared Shell v1 → Community adapter/config**



That is the terminal architecture I would aim for.

The shared shell can own a proven dropdown component without requiring every consumer to instantiate every menu. For Chatcenter 2.0 release we might truthfully expose only:



**Chatboards ▾** | **Lesson Plans ▾** | account/notifications

Later, adding Jobs is a navigation configuration change, not another shell redesign.



## Responsive behavior



This is another reason to converge now.



We should **stop independently solving Community responsive header collapse**. The Job Center Shell Lab already has a mature solution. The convergence acceptance should say:



> preserve Community content priorities, but adopt the canonical Shared Shell responsive behavior wherever shell behavior is concerned.

Community owns what happens to its **rails/feed** below the shell; Shared Shell owns what happens to the **navbar/header/footer**.



## Recommended workflow posture



This is a real **CONVERGENCE objective**, because it crosses repositories, CSS ownership, responsive behavior, component behavior, and design authority. But I would keep Codex at **Luna/Medium initially**. The first cycle is evidence/reconciliation, not difficult implementation.



Only escalate if inspection reveals contradictory shell owners or no clean extraction boundary.



The sequence I recommend is therefore:



**1. Finish bell glyph → close Newskin header visual objective.**  

**2. Shared Shell v1 reconciliation diagnostic.**  

**3. Engineering Director approves the token/component/ownership contract.**  

**4. Extract/establish canonical shared shell.**  

**5. Community consumes it while preserving its accepted inner geometry.**  

**6. Verify dropdowns + responsive behavior + footer.**  

**7. Reconcile Job Center back onto the same canonical source.**

## Step 1 — Define the jobs of the Community page

| 2 | **Get the user into a conversation** | replies, likes, posts |

| 3 | **Bring them back to personally relevant activity** | retention/return habit |

| 4 | **Help them discover communities and discussions** | deeper session/pageviews |

| 5 | **Expose useful Teachers.Net ecosystem content** | Jobs/Lessons/etc. without distracting |

| 6 | **Monetize the journey** | strong viewability without damaging #1–5 |



That ranking should govern the rails—not vice versa.

- **Recommended Chatboards**

- **New discussions**

- **Unanswered questions** — particularly compelling for a teacher community: *“Help a teacher out.”*

Future possibilities we should leave open:



- responsive/mobile ad inventory;

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-001073-A — ASSISTANT

I agree with the direction, and I think **X provides the strongest model for Teachers.Net's creation journey**, while Facebook provides a useful lesson about initial friction.



The important distinction is between **discoverability** and **composer persistence**. We want creation to be obvious at first load, but we do not need to permanently consume valuable feed real estate with the entire composer.



## I would change our model



Instead of treating the current inline composer as the actual editor:



> avatar + “What do you want to ask teachers?” + Post



treat it as a **composer launcher**.



On fresh Home load it remains exactly where users expect it, immediately above the feed. Clicking anywhere on it opens the real composer as a modal.



That gives us Facebook's excellent initial discoverability with X's better full composition environment.



### Why modal is better for Teachers.Net



Our posting model is potentially richer than a short social post.



A teacher may want to:



- write several paragraphs;

- attach an image;

- paste a URL and preview it;

- select a destination Chatboard;

- potentially add other structured information later.



Trying to make all of that expand inline pushes the feed downward and creates substantial layout state.



A modal gives us a stable workspace.



It also solves another problem we've discussed: **Home is broader than a Chatboard**. A Home composer eventually needs to know:



> Where should this be posted?



That is much easier to handle elegantly in a modal than in a little inline bar.



## Persistent creation: one secondary controller



I don't think we need Threads' two persistent mechanisms.



We have something Threads doesn't: a substantial global Shared Shell plus potentially a left rail.



My preferred hierarchy:



### Initial viewport



Prominent center launcher:



**[avatar] What do you want to ask or share?**



No separate giant `Start a New Topic` left card.



### While scrolling — full desktop with left rail



A single persistent:



**＋ Post**



or perhaps



**✎ Post**



button in the left rail.



This is where X's model is excellent. It is extremely obvious without interfering with the feed.



And it gives the left rail a persistent high-value action rather than a giant introductory card.



Something like:



**YOUR CHATBOARDS**  

...  



**DISCOVER**  

...



**[ ＋ Post ]**



But I would actually put Post **near the top**, not below everything:



> **＋ Post**

>

> Your Chatboards  

> Discover



That parallels Gmail's Compose and X's Post: creation is an action, not navigation.



### Once the left rail disappears



The same semantic action becomes a **floating compose button** at bottom-right.



That pattern is already extremely well trained by Facebook, Threads and many mobile apps.



So:



**desktop:** labeled rail button  

**constrained/feed-only:** floating icon button  

**mobile:** floating compose button, unless our compact navigation eventually provides a better persistent slot.



One creation action, different responsive representations.



## I prefer `Post` over `Start a New Topic`



Especially on Home.



`Start a New Topic` is Chatboards terminology.



Home is becoming broader.



**Post** is concise and trained by essentially every social system.



When the modal opens, *then* we can ask the necessary Community-specific question:



**Post to:**  

`Main Teachers Chatboard ▾`



Perhaps intelligently defaulted from context.



If a user invokes Post while inside the AI in Education Chatboard, destination defaults to AI in Education.



If invoked from Home, use their appropriate default or require destination selection.



That gives us one platform creation interaction without pretending every Teachers.Net object is the same.



## The modal itself



I would borrow heavily from X's conceptual structure but retain our visual language.



Something like:



```text

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ ×                                      Drafts        │

│                                                      │

│ [avatar]  What do you want to ask or share?          │

│                                                      │

│                                                      │

│                                                      │

│ Post to:  Main Teachers Chatboard ▾                  │

│ ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── │

│ 🖼  Link/media tools                    [ Post ]      │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```



Not necessarily those exact controls.



The important anatomy is:



**identity → composition → destination → attachments/options → Post**



And because it's modal, we can grow this later without redesigning Home.



## This also lets us simplify the left rail further



Our previous proposed `CREATE` card:



- Start a New Topic

- Ask a Question

- Share a Resource



now feels too heavy.



Those are probably **composer modes**, not three permanent Home navigation items.



One **Post** button can open the modal.



Inside it, we might eventually have:



**Discussion | Question | Resource**



if those distinctions actually matter to downstream behavior.



Don't make users choose among three creation destinations before they've even started expressing themselves.



## There is a useful product distinction here



The persistent action should be:



> **Post**



not:



> **Compose**



Gmail composes because the object is an email.



Teachers.Net posts because the object enters a social/public stream.



And the initial prompt:



> **What do you want to ask or share?**



is better than generic “What's happening?” because it reinforces Teachers.Net's purpose.



## Revised Home structure



This makes our full desktop substantially quieter:



```text

LEFT                    CENTER                         RIGHT



[ + Post ]              [avatar] Ask or share...      Continue Conversation



Your Chatboards          For You Following Latest      [ 300×250 ]

• Main

• AI                     Discussion                    New Jobs

• NBPTS

• Kindergarten           Discussion                    Featured Lesson



Discover                 Discussion

• Trending

• Unanswered             ...

• Browse

                         Discussion #10



                         [ 728×90 ]



                         Discussion #11

```



That feels much closer to the restraint we're seeing in the successful social products.



And now every persistent surface has a clear reason to exist:



- **Header:** global product navigation.

- **Left:** create + personalized Community navigation.

- **Center:** consumption/participation.

- **Right:** return behavior + monetization + restrained cross-product discovery.

- **Floating Post:** creation continuity when left rail disappears.



I would lock this as our **creation hypothesis** for the Home mockup:



> **Initial inline-looking launcher → modal composer; persistent labeled Post action while the rail exists → floating compose action after the rail retires.**



That should be in the next render because it materially changes how sparse and intentional the left rail can become.

A subject line made perfect sense on Teachers.Net chatboards because users were scanning a **topic index**. There, `Brand new post!` is the thing you're selecting.



But Home isn't a topic index anymore. It's a consumption stream.



Look at your Facebook example. The visual hierarchy is roughly:



**NBC 7 San Diego** ✓  

`8 hours ago · 🌐`



> The coins, which can be used as legal tender...



**[large media]**



Then the linked object's own headline appears *inside the link attachment*, where it belongs.



There isn't another:



> **Heads or tails!**



headline sitting between the author and the post.



That's substantially more natural for a feed.



## I think Home should treat our legacy subject as contextual metadata



We don't necessarily remove subjects from the underlying Community model. They're still useful for:



- individual discussion pages;

- Chatboard/topic listings;

- URLs/search;

- notifications;

- SEO;

- legacy compatibility.



But **Home doesn't necessarily need to render them as headlines**.



For a post like:



> **Brand new post!**  

> This is a brand new post - testing it!!!



Home could simply render:



**Bob R/CA** · 13m  

Teachers Chatboard



> This is a brand new post — testing it!!!



○ Reply   ♡ Like



That instantly becomes a social object rather than a directory entry.



For a richer post:



**Bob R/CA** · Aug 29  

AI in Education



> Bounded local YouTube...



**[YouTube preview]**



○ Reply   ♡ Like



Again, the media supplies its own headline.



### Author should absolutely move to the top



I agree that this is the strongest common pattern across the models we've examined.



The user's eye should encounter:



**avatar → Bob R/CA**



before:



`TEACHERS CHATBOARD · 248 members · ★`



Our current card makes the **container/community** more prominent than the human being who said something. That's backwards for Home.



I'd invert it:



```text

[avatar]  Bob R/CA                         ···

          Teachers Chatboard · 13m



This is a brand new post — testing it!!!



💬 Reply        ♡ Like

```



Or perhaps:



```text

[avatar]  Bob R/CA · 13m                   ···

          Teachers Chatboard



This is a brand new post — testing it!!!

```



The Chatboard is useful provenance, but it should be visually secondary.



## Member count probably doesn't belong on every Home card



`248 members` is useful when evaluating whether to **join or visit a Chatboard**.



It adds almost nothing when reading Bob's post.



Likewise the gold star appears to represent a Chatboard relationship/action rather than the post itself. We should question whether that belongs in every feed card at all.



This is precisely why the page currently looks simultaneously **clean and busy**: there are many tiny pieces of metadata, but none creates strong visual hierarchy.



Removing weak metadata may make the cards feel *richer*, not emptier.



## Views are questionable too



Facebook doesn't show impressions/views on ordinary text posts in this consumption context. Threads doesn't generally make views one of the primary social actions either.



For Teachers.Net:



**Replies** are socially meaningful.  

**Likes** are socially meaningful.  

**Views** are mostly publisher analytics/social proof.



`0 views` especially contributes almost nothing.



I would strongly consider removing views from the Home card engagement row.



Then the footer can become actual actions rather than a stats report:



**💬 Reply     ♡ Like**



with counts attached when nonzero.



That gives us bigger targets and considerably more breathing room.



## The body should become the star



This is probably the biggest visual improvement.



Right now:



- blue Chatboard name;

- member count;

- star;

- big blue subject;

- byline;

- body;

- rule;

- tiny engagement.



The user's actual words are buried about fifth in hierarchy.



I'd reverse that:



1. **Human identity**

2. secondary context/time

3. **actual post**

4. media/link

5. social actions



That's it.



And that addresses your “wash of white” observation in an interesting way: I don't think the answer is necessarily adding backgrounds, shadows, or colored furniture.



Facebook's feed is mostly white too.



What makes it legible is **strong content hierarchy**.



The avatar/identity anchors the upper-left. Text is given meaningful scale and space. Media becomes dominant when present. Engagement forms a recognizable lower boundary. Then the next human identity starts the next object.



### Subjects could still appear selectively



There may be cases where the subject carries meaning not repeated in the body.



Rather than blindly deleting it, we could define Home presentation semantics:



**Normal discussion:** subject suppressed; body leads.



**Question:** perhaps the subject becomes the question when the body is supporting detail.



**Link/media:** attachment owns its headline.



**Job/Lesson insertion:** those structured objects absolutely retain titles because their title is intrinsic product data.



This would create richer variation in the unified feed without preserving a 1990s message-board convention universally.



## I would also question card borders eventually



Not yet—but look at Facebook.



The feed object is separated primarily through spacing and background context rather than every post being a thin blue-gray rectangle.



Threads goes even further: horizontal separators, essentially no card furniture.



Our rounded outlined rectangles contribute to the “stack of database records” feeling.



Once we fix hierarchy, we may discover we want:



- much subtler borders;

- perhaps separators rather than cards;

- slightly stronger page/background contrast;

- larger avatars;

- more generous content typography.



But I would **not decide that until we render the new anatomy**. The existing card container might look excellent once the inside stops behaving like a topic listing.



### My provisional Home discussion anatomy



I think this is the next design target:



```text

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│ [avatar]  Bob R/CA                              ··· │

│           Teachers Chatboard · 13m                  │

│                                                     │

│ This is a brand new post — testing it!!!            │

│                                                     │

│ [ media / OG / YouTube when present ]               │

│                                                     │

│ 💬 Reply  12                         ♡ Like  18      │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```



No prominent subject.  

No member count.  

No views.  

No star unless we discover a compelling post-level purpose for it.



That would be a fairly radical simplification of the current card, but paradoxically I think it would make the feed feel **far more alive**, because the thing jumping out repeatedly would be:



**Bob said this. Alison said this. Jennifer shared this.**



rather than:



**Teachers Chatboard / 248 members / QA notification...**



That's exactly the psychological shift we want if `teachers.net/` is becoming a daily social/professional Home.

### What it proved



This was **not actually a timezone defect**. The timestamp chain is correct:

The problem was simply **loss of precision in presentation**. The formatter converted, for example, 13h11m and 13h42m into the same `13 hours` label. 



Codex now produces:



- 15:55 post → **13 hours 11 minutes**

- 15:50 → **13 hours 16 minutes**

- 15:45 → **13 hours 21 minutes**

- 15:40 → **13 hours 25 minutes**

- 15:24 → **13 hours 42 minutes**

- Sep 1 content → **Sep 1**



Those values were checked against the stored timestamps and the actual current Pacific time. 



Only `page-newskin.php` changed. No timestamps, feed ordering, Shared Shell, cards, or production data changed. Commit `28e4440` is pushed. 



### My disposition



**Temporal correctness: PASS.**



I don't think you need to spend a manual QA cycle verifying the arithmetic unless you want to. The state/data evidence is decisive enough.



I would, however, distinguish **correctness from final presentation**. `13 hours 42 minutes` is truthful, but we may ultimately prefer something terser such as `13h` or `13h 42m`. That's a card-design decision, not a temporal defect. We should settle it during the card redesign rather than reopening this formatter diagnosis.



So we can carry forward:



> **Home timestamp source, timezone interpretation, and relative-age arithmetic — PROVEN.**



And move directly to the more interesting objective we just outlined: **redesign the Home discussion card around the poster and content rather than the legacy topic-index hierarchy.**



Given that this is now subjective visual/product work rather than causal uncertainty, I would also follow Codex's recommendation and **return to Luna / Normal** for the first implementation/render pass.

Yes. Looking across these eight captures, there is a surprisingly strong **common grammar** despite major differences in branding and product philosophy. That gives us useful evidence for separating mature conventions from arbitrary stylistic choices.



## 1. The strongest consensus: the author owns the post



This is nearly universal across Facebook, Bluesky, Instagram, Mastodon, Tumblr and X.



The basic opening grammar is:



> **[avatar] Author identity · time**  

> content



Not:



> community/category  

> subject  

> author  

> content



Reddit is the notable exception because Reddit is deliberately **community/topic-centric** rather than primarily identity-centric. Even there, the subreddit/source and time form a compact provenance row immediately associated with the post rather than several levels of metadata.



This strongly supports changing Teachers.Net Home from:



> TEACHERS CHATBOARD · 248 members · ★  

> **Brand new post!**  

> by Bob R/CA · Sep 3  

> body



to something much closer to:



> **Bob R/CA** · 13 hours ago  

> Teachers Chatboard  

>

> This is a brand new post — testing it!!!



That's probably our highest-confidence finding.



---



## 2. Subjects/headlines are the exception, not the default



Your earlier observation holds across the larger sample.



**Facebook:** ordinary user posts have no subject.



**Bluesky:** no subject.



**Instagram:** no subject.



**Mastodon:** no subject.



**Tumblr:** no required subject.



**X:** no subject.



Reddit is again the exception because the Reddit post object is explicitly constructed around a title.



External linked content is different. Across these products, **the linked object may carry a headline inside its own attachment card**. Mastodon and Bluesky demonstrate that particularly clearly in these captures.



That argues strongly for:



> **Suppress legacy Teachers.Net subject on ordinary Home discussion cards.**



Not delete it from Community. It remains useful for the topic page, Chatboard listings, URLs/search, notifications, SEO, etc.



Home simply doesn't need to elevate it.



---



## 3. There is very little metadata



This is striking when compared with our current card.



The successful systems generally want enough metadata to answer:



**Who said this?**  

**When?**  

**What context do I need?**



Then they stop.



Our current card has:



- Chatboard

- membership count

- star

- subject

- author

- date/time

- body

- replies

- views

- likes



before considering media.



That's why our feed can simultaneously look sparse **and** information-heavy. We have lots of low-emphasis information competing for attention.



### Strong candidate removals from Home



- `248 members`

- star

- prominent subject

- probably views



Those data can remain elsewhere.



---



# 4. Content is given substantially more typographic authority



Another strong pattern.



The actual user text isn't presented like tertiary metadata. It is the purpose of the object.



Facebook's fishing example is almost comically simple:



> **Cory Brown · 12 hours ago**  

>

> Are there any spots in La Jolla to fish from shore?



That's the card.



Our equivalent currently would probably put several lines of structural metadata above that question.



Bluesky, Mastodon and Tumblr similarly allow ordinary prose to occupy substantial visual territory.



For Teachers.Net—where discussion and professional advice are often text-heavy—this matters even more.



I'd increase our body text modestly and give it much stronger contrast.



---



## 5. Media changes the entire visual center of gravity



Another near-universal convention:



**Text-only post:** text is dominant.



**Image/video post:** media becomes dominant.



**Link post:** attachment becomes a contained object beneath the author's text.



The surrounding card doesn't compete.



Instagram is the extreme case: media essentially *is* the post.



Facebook gives media almost the entire card width.



X, Bluesky, Mastodon and Tumblr all allow rich media to become substantially larger than our current right-aligned thumbnail treatment.



This is one area where I think our existing Newskin cards are materially behind the model.



Our current YouTube/OG presentation tends toward:



> text on left | little media box on right



That's an **article-list/index pattern**.



The dominant feed pattern is:



> post text  

>

> **large media/attachment beneath it**



That's a significant future change I'd put high on the ledger.



---



# 6. Engagement actions are extraordinarily consistent



The icon language varies, but the semantic set is remarkably stable.



Across the platforms we see some combination of:



**Reply / Comment**  

**Like / Favorite / Vote**  

**Repost / Share**  

**Save / Bookmark**  

**More ···**



Teachers.Net doesn't need to implement all of those simply because competitors do.



Our existing meaningful actions are basically:



**Reply**  

**Like**



Those are enough for v1.



But their **presentation should look like actions**, not analytics.



Current:



> ◯ Be the first to reply     ◎ 0 views     ♡ Like



I'd move toward:



> 💬 Reply          ♡ Like



and incorporate counts naturally when they exist.



### Views



X exposes views because it has made impressions part of its public engagement vocabulary.



Most others don't make ordinary views a core interaction.



I remain inclined to remove Views from Home. We can still track them.



---



# 7. `···` is essentially universal



This may be the strongest small convention in the sample.



The upper-right or action row contains a More menu across:



- Facebook

- Bluesky

- Instagram

- Mastodon

- Reddit

- Tumblr

- X



That is extremely well trained.



Teachers.Net should probably adopt it.



We don't need to populate it heavily initially. Legitimate items might eventually include:



- Save

- Follow discussion

- Hide

- Report

- Copy link



with permissions adding Edit/Delete for one's own content.



But `···` gives us an extensible home for secondary actions without contaminating the primary card.



---



# 8. Cards themselves differ considerably



This is where there is **no consensus**, which is useful.



**Facebook:** discrete rounded white card against gray canvas.



**Bluesky:** essentially rows separated by horizontal rules.



**X:** continuous white column with separators.



**Mastodon:** outlined/sectioned feed.



**Instagram:** extremely minimal furniture.



**Tumblr:** obvious cards against a strongly contrasting background.



**Reddit:** mostly row/separator architecture in this capture.



So we should **not infer that removing our card border is some industry requirement**.



The consensus is about **internal anatomy**, not container decoration.



I'd keep our existing subtle card temporarily, redesign its contents, and then judge whether the border still helps.



---



# 9. Avatar size is meaningful



Across these systems, avatar + identity creates a strong visual rhythm down the left edge of the feed.



Our avatar isn't disastrously small, but the surrounding hierarchy currently prevents it from doing its job.



I would test approximately **44–48px** for ordinary Home cards.



That creates:



> face  

> face  

> face  

> face



down the feed—which is psychologically important. It reinforces that Teachers.Net is populated by **people**, not topic records.



---



# 10. Community provenance should remain—but quietly



Teachers.Net isn't exactly Facebook or X.



Our Chatboards have real meaning.



A teacher may care whether something came from:



**Kindergarten Teachers**  

**NBPTS**  

**AI in Education**



So I wouldn't remove Chatboard identity.



I'd demote it.



Perhaps:



> **Bob R/CA** · 3 hours ago  

> in **AI in Education**



or:



> **Bob R/CA** · 3 hours ago  

> **AI in Education**



That gives Home context without allowing taxonomy to overpower the person.



This is one place where Teachers.Net can productively differ from generic social networks.



---



# 11. The platforms separate post identity from attachment identity



This is important for our OG work.



For example:



> **Bob R/CA** · 2h  

> AI in Education

>

> This is a fascinating piece about...

>

> ┌────────────────────────────┐

> │ IMAGE                      │

> │                            │

> │ Article headline           │

> │ Publisher · description    │

> └────────────────────────────┘



The article title belongs to **the attachment**, not to Bob's post.



This reinforces our earlier conclusion that the legacy Teachers.Net subject should not compete with the OG headline.



---



# 12. Feed width is used for content, not metadata



This may become significant later.



Our 728px center is currently occupied by a lot of horizontal metadata arrangements and right-side previews.



These competitors overwhelmingly use their center width to make:



- prose comfortable;

- photographs large;

- video large;

- link cards substantial.



That suggests our 728 width is actually quite valuable once we stop filling it with directory-style structure.

2. **Avatar prominent.**

> **AI in Education**

> **Bob R/CA** · 2h  

> post body...



No repeated Chatboard name.

## 2. Short text deserves a distinct presentation mode



Facebook's treatment is compelling.



A short statement or question can otherwise look visually weak compared with image/video cards. Their solution is essentially:



> **short content → allow content itself to become the visual**



I think Teachers.Net should absolutely explore this.



Your proposed threshold of roughly **95 characters** is a good modeling reference, but I wouldn't lock Facebook's exact threshold before seeing our typography and width. The product rule matters more than the exact number:



### Standard text mode



Longer post:



> normal readable feed typography



### Short-emphasis mode



Short post/question:



> substantially larger text  

> generous vertical space  

> possibly centered or stronger composition



Example:



> **Does anyone still give homework on weekends?**



That deserves to punch through the feed much more strongly than a normal paragraph setting would.



### Background mode



I also like offering backgrounds later.



But I'd treat that as an **author-selected presentation feature**, not something automatically added by the feed.



The key distinction:



- automatic: short text gets improved typography;

- optional future feature: author chooses a background/style in the composer.



That avoids turning every 40-character post into a carnival card.

I agree with your correction.



We shouldn't interpret:



> “don't fabricate unsupported actions in v1”



as:



> “Teachers.Net doesn't need them.”



The mature feed interaction set is now effectively a product expectation:



- **Reply**

- **Like**

- **Repost / Share**

- **Save / Bookmark**

- **More**



Teachers.Net should ultimately support all of these.



What we are deciding is sequencing.



### v1 card surface



Primary visible actions:



**Reply**  

**Like**



Potentially later visible:



**Share**



### `···` secondary menu



I like your proposed set:



1. **Save**

2. **Follow discussion**

3. **Hide**

4. **Report**

5. **Copy link**



Then contextual ownership actions:



- **Edit**

- **Delete**



Those last two are foundational, not luxuries. They belong in the system as soon as the underlying authorization and persistence contracts are ready.



The `···` menu is particularly valuable because it lets us grow functionality without cluttering the action row.



---



# 4. We should distinguish actions from analytics



The comparison set reinforces this.



For Teachers.Net Home, I'd separate:



### Interaction

- Reply

- Like

- Share

- Save



### Analytics

- Views



Views may still be useful in a discussion-detail page, author's own post analytics, admin/moderation, or some Chatboard views.



But I remain unconvinced that `0 views` belongs in every Home card.



The other platforms that expose views prominently tend to have explicitly trained users around that metric. Teachers.Net hasn't.

# 5. Dedicated Chatboard page now has a clearer role



These Facebook/Reddit captures also help us distinguish **Home** from **Chatboards**.



### Home



Mixed-channel social/professional stream.



Card shows:



- author

- time

- Chatboard provenance

- content

- media

- social actions



### Dedicated Chatboard



The surrounding page owns:



- Chatboard name

- description

- membership/join state

- Chatboard navigation

- perhaps highlights/pinned content

- composer



Cards then become simpler:



- author

- time

- content

- media

- actions



This is a very strong architecture because it prevents us from forcing every piece of community context into every feed object.



---



# 6. Reddit gives us one caution about subjects



Reddit does still use titles heavily.



But that's because Reddit's submission model makes the title an intrinsic part of the post object.



Teachers.Net legacy Chatboards behave somewhat similarly.



So I wouldn't say:



> subjects are obsolete everywhere.



I'd say:



> **subjects are no longer appropriate as the dominant representation of ordinary posts on Teachers.Net Home.**



We can retain them where they add structural value:



- dedicated topic pages;

- Chatboard topic indexes;

- search results;

- notifications;

- perhaps some question-format posts.



The Home card can suppress them by default.



That preserves backward compatibility without letting legacy architecture dictate modern presentation.



---



# 7. Facebook's Group cards suggest another useful feature



Notice how the group feed surfaces **selected comments directly under a post**.



That's potentially very relevant to Teachers.Net because conversation is our core product.



A future Home card might show:



> post  

> Reply · Like  

>

> **Jennifer M.** This worked really well with my 7th graders.  

> **Bob R/CA** That's exactly what I was wondering...



Not every post, not every comment, and not necessarily v1.



But one or two relevant/recent comments can make a feed feel dramatically more alive.



This may be more valuable to Teachers.Net than some of the extra metadata we've historically shown.



I would put **inline comment preview** onto the future-card ledger.



---



## Revised card rules I'd now record



The research is converging enough that I would carry forward these as strong candidates:



- **Author is always the primary card identity.**

- **Mixed Home feed shows Chatboard provenance.**

- **Dedicated Chatboard feed suppresses repeated Chatboard provenance.**

- **Ordinary Home cards suppress legacy subject/title by default.**

- **Short text gets an emphasized typography mode.**

- **Optional author-selected backgrounds are a future composer capability.**

- **Long text stays in normal feed typography.**

- **Media occupies the main feed width beneath text.**

- **Reply + Like are current primary actions.**

- **Share/Repost + Save are required future capabilities, not discarded ideas.**

- **`···` becomes the standard home for Save / Follow / Hide / Report / Copy link and contextual Edit/Delete.**

- **Views probably leave ordinary Home cards.**

- **Inline comment previews deserve later consideration because conversation is central to Teachers.Net.**

- **Dedicated Chatboard pages should carry community identity at the page level, allowing simpler cards.**



At this point the **parent-card anatomy is largely converged**. The two areas I would still study before rendering are:



1. **how much of the comments/replies to expose directly in Home**, and  

2. **how the short-text emphasis mode should visually behave inside our 728-ish center width**.



Those are now the two biggest unresolved pieces rather than basic card hierarchy.
