Yes—I can reach the Google page, and this research materially changes how I'd think about Home monetization.



The short version is: **your instinct is right. We have been thinking too much in the old fixed-IAB-unit world. Modern publisher infrastructure explicitly supports feed-native, fluid and responsive inventory.** The 728×90 remains commercially useful, but it no longer needs to determine our product geometry.



## What Google's current inventory guidance says



The page you linked still identifies these as Google's top-performing conventional sizes:



- **728×90** leaderboard — lots of advertiser inventory; Google specifically mentions forums.

- **336×280** large rectangle.

- **300×250** medium rectangle.

- **300×50** mobile banner.

- **160×600** wide skyscraper. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/admanager/answer/1100453))



And your concern about narrower horizontal alternatives is justified. Google supports `468×60`, but explicitly warns that available supply is generally more limited and performance can therefore be suboptimal. `970×90` and `970×250` go the other direction—larger, not useful for our feed. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/admanager/answer/1100453))



So if we restrict ourselves to **fixed-size display**, there's no magical ~600×100 unit waiting to solve our problem.



But that's no longer the whole market.



## The industry has explicitly moved beyond fixed pixels



The IAB's New Ad Portfolio replaced the older desktop/mobile creative guidelines with **aspect-ratio and size-range based flexible units**. The stated goal is cross-screen production and integration with responsive site design rather than forcing sites around fixed pixel dimensions. ([IAB Tech Lab](https://iabtechlab.com/standards/iab-new-ad-portfolio-guidelines/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))



That's almost exactly the architectural problem we're confronting.



Instead of:



> “Which standard rectangle should Teachers.Net's feed be built around?”



the contemporary question is:



> **“What is the publisher's content container, and what eligible creative can transact successfully inside it?”**



That's a major difference.



---



# More importantly: Google has a product specifically for what we're building



Google defines a feed as a scrollable stream of repeating content blocks and explicitly gives a **homepage main feed/news feed** as an example. It supports different feed/ad treatments on desktop and mobile. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/admanager/answer/9189559?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



Then it provides **In-feed ads** specifically for that environment.



Google describes them as native units placed between feed content, designed to match the site's look and feel and avoid breaking the user's flow. It explicitly calls out their suitability for mobile. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/adsense/answer/9189557?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



That is essentially the Facebook example you just showed me.



And there's an important implementation detail:



### Fluid native



Google Ad Manager supports a `Fluid` native size.



Rather than requesting:



> `728 × 90`



we provide a container.



The native ad **fills the width of that enclosing column and determines its appropriate height**. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/admanager/answer/9178980?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



So if our ideal Teachers.Net card turns out to be:



**640px**



or:



**660px**



or:



**680px**



we don't necessarily need to hunt for an advertiser buying precisely `660×whatever`.



A fluid native placement can occupy that feed geometry.



That is the piece that substantially changes my recommendation.



---



# Buyers can still bring display demand into that hole



There's another important nuance.



Google says native In-feed inventory uses creatives with high-quality ad elements, including responsive Google Ads creatives. But Google also lets publishers enable **selected display ads inside In-feed units**, choosing display creatives that fit the available space.



Google specifically says this can help increase revenue because native-only In-feed CPM can be lower in the short term for some publishers. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/adsense/answer/9189557?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



So we're not necessarily choosing:



> native beautiful feed ads **or** high-fill display.



There is a hybrid demand strategy available.



That's very relevant for Teachers.Net.



---



# What media buyers increasingly want



I would divide buyer demand into three buckets.



### 1. Commodity display



Still enormous and useful.



That's where:



- 300×250

- 336×280

- 728×90

- 300×600

- etc.



continue to matter.



We should absolutely retain commercially valuable conventional inventory where it doesn't hurt the product.



Our **right-rail 300×250** remains a very defensible example.



### 2. Responsive display



Advertisers increasingly provide assets rather than one finished fixed-size banner:



- logo;

- images;

- headlines;

- descriptions;

- CTA;

- potentially video.



The serving system assembles those into available inventory.



That is naturally suited to responsive publisher layouts.



### 3. Native/in-feed



This is particularly aligned with:



- social streams;

- article feeds;

- news homepages;

- recommendation streams;

- product/listing feeds.



The advertiser supplies structured assets and the **publisher controls the presentation grammar**.



That's why Facebook's ALDI advertisement looks like a Facebook post rather than a 1998 banner dropped between Facebook posts.



---



# There's a fill-rate caveat



You anticipated it correctly.



Native/fluid inventory can have different economics from standardized high-demand display inventory. Google itself acknowledges that In-feed/native can produce **lower CPM in the short term for some publishers**, which is why it supports selected display demand in those slots. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/adsense/answer/9189557?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



So I would not tell you:



> “Native feed ads definitely make more money.”



We don't know that.



But we can architect Teachers.Net so we can **measure it instead of guessing**.



---



# Cadence: we can be much more conservative than the platforms



Google permits multiple In-feed ads and recommends at least **three content blocks between ads**. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/adsense/answer/9189037?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



That doesn't mean we should run one every fourth card.



Our instinct of roughly **one sponsored object per 8–10 organic feed objects initially** is deliberately conservative.



That's where I'd start.



If engagement remains strong and economics justify increasing frequency, we can test 8, 6, etc.



Do not start at maximum monetization pressure.



---



# User tolerance has a measurable boundary too



The Coalition for Better Ads updated its standards in 2026 after new research with more than 55,000 respondents. For desktop web, ad density over **50%** is now specifically identified as a poor experience; mobile remains substantially less tolerant, with >30% density among the problematic experiences. ([Better Ads](https://www.betterads.org/blog/cba-updates-desktop-mobile-web-standards?utm_source=chatgpt.com))



They also continue to identify things like:



- large sticky ads;

- autoplay video with sound;

- intrusive popups/prestitials



as objectionable experiences. ([Better Ads](https://www.betterads.org/standards/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))



We're nowhere near a 50% density with a 1:10 feed cadence, obviously, but the principle is useful:



> **Monetize consumption; don't obstruct consumption.**



---



# What I would now architect for Teachers.Net



I think our Home monetization model should become:



### Full desktop



**Right rail**

- 300×250 conventional display.

- High-fill conventional inventory.

- Visible early.

- Doesn't dictate center geometry.



**Center**

- beautiful content-led social feed;

- feed width chosen entirely for UX;

- fluid/native sponsored object every ~8–10 organic objects initially.



### Constrained desktop



When the right rail retires:



- 300×250 disappears;

- center feed remains unchanged;

- native/fluid sponsored inventory continues.



We no longer have the problem of finding somewhere awkward to relocate the rectangle.



### Mobile



- same conceptual feed;

- separate mobile In-feed configuration if appropriate;

- responsive native fills the actual content width.



Google specifically recommends separate In-feed units when desktop and mobile feed styles differ. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/adsense/answer/9189037?hl=en&utm_source=chatgpt.com))



That is exactly what ours will do.



---

This research gives me enough confidence to make that recommendation stronger.



**Don't delete the 728 inventory from Teachers.Net globally.**



It's still a top-performing standard format, Google still says it has abundant advertiser inventory, and other Teachers.Net surfaces may remain excellent homes for it. ([Google Support](https://support.google.com/admanager/answer/1100453))



Job Center, Lesson Plans, legacy forums, article pages and other layouts can make independent monetization decisions.



But:



> **I would no longer put a 728×90 requirement into the Home Feed v1 geometry contract.**



Home is becoming a modern feed product. It should use modern feed monetization.



## Proposed Home ad architecture



| State | Right rail | Feed |

|---|---|---|

| Full desktop | **300×250 display** | Fluid/native sponsored card |

| Constrained desktop | retired | Fluid/native sponsored card |

| Tablet | none | Responsive/native sponsored card |

| Mobile | none | Mobile In-feed/native |

| Other TNet products | product-specific | 728 etc. remain available |



And critically, we should instrument each separately:



**fill rate · eCPM · viewability · revenue/session · scroll depth · session duration · cards consumed · return rate**



The real optimization target isn't highest CPM.



It's closer to:



> **revenue per engaged Home session without degrading the behavior that creates those sessions.**



That's the modern publisher problem—and the card-feed architecture finally gives Teachers.Net the right substrate for solving it.

### Repost



Repost is a Teachers.Net-native social object and deserves separate product design.

**Repost**

**Quote**

> create a new post by me containing Bob's canonical post as an inset object, with my own commentary above it.



That touches attribution, deletion/edit behavior, notifications, counts, feed ranking, canonical identity, permissions and probably moderation. Not terribly exotic, but materially more than Share.



So I'd sequence:



**Share → Save → Follow discussion → Repost → Quote**



while Edit/Delete proceeds on its own necessary authorization track.

- Feed scroll position can remain intact.

- `X` has an obvious trained meaning.

- We can display the original post and conversation context without forcing a navigation.

For **Home engagement**, the modal is stronger.

- `💬 Reply` — zero

### CHATGPT-9356b0f0ac-001176-A — ASSISTANT

I think this exposes a **real product-model decision**, and I would settle it before visually refining the modal because it determines what the modal is representing.



My recommendation is:



> **Move Teachers.Net Community 3.0 to subjectless posts everywhere by default—including Group/Chatboard feeds. Preserve legacy subjects as historical metadata, not as a required element of the new posting model.**



The distinction is between **channel context** and **post title**.



### Why I think subjects should go



Our closest analogues divide fairly cleanly:



- Facebook Groups: group supplies the context; individual posts generally have no title.

- Threads: no titles.

- X: no titles.

- Bluesky: no titles.

- Mastodon: no ordinary title.

- Instagram: no titles.

- Reddit is the major exception—and Reddit is structurally much more of a **link/topic index → discussion page** product. Titles are fundamental to browsing Reddit.



Teachers.Net historically resembled Reddit more:



> Chatboard → list of subjects → open topic → discussion.



But the Home we're building changes the fundamental consumption model:



> feed → consume post directly → interact in place.



A mandatory subject becomes redundant overhead in that model.



And on a dedicated Chatboard:



> **AI in Education**  

> Bob: “Artificial intelligence is changing education…”



already establishes both dimensions needed to understand the object. Requiring Bob to additionally write:



> **How AI is changing education**



doesn't add much.



### There are cases where titles remain useful



I wouldn't abolish the concept from the data model.



Some Teachers.Net objects legitimately benefit from titles:



- long-form resources;

- Lessons;

- Jobs;

- Projects;

- perhaps future articles;

- imported/legacy discussions;

- potentially an explicitly supported long-form Community post type someday.



But **ordinary Community post** shouldn't require one.



That also makes composition friction substantially lower:



> “What's on your mind?”



rather than:



> Subject: ______  

> Message: ______



which matters if we're trying to increase posting.



## Legacy subjects should survive gracefully



This modal is an excellent example.



The post currently contains:



**QA notification reply journey 2026-09-01**  

then the same title again  

then body.



That's far too much hierarchy.



For a legacy titled discussion I would render something more like:

│ This is a fresh reply...                   │

No separate modal title repeating the subject.

because the actual post immediately presents that information.

What started as **“make Home behave like a modern feed”** has exposed a better near-term architecture for the entire legacy Community system. We should stop treating `/newskin/` as a special presentation and instead treat it as the **reference consumer for a shared legacy-Community presentation layer**.



The good news is that the hardest seams are already being proven. The modal reads canonical discussion data from `tnet_chatposts`, writes replies through the existing `tnetcomment` owner, preserves notifications downstream, and leaves canonical legacy discussion URLs independently viable.  That means we are not contemplating a data migration or a second Community backend. This can largely be a **consumer migration over the existing authoritative system**.



## The architecture I would aim for



There should ultimately be one legacy-Community presentation system serving two primary contexts:



**Mixed/Home feed**



```text

Home

  └─ posts from many Chatboards

       ├─ author-first card

       ├─ specialized-board provenance pill when needed

       ├─ subjectless new posts

       ├─ legacy title displayed gracefully when present

       └─ Reply → modal discussion

```



**Dedicated Chatboard**



```text

AI in Education

  └─ same post/card system

       ├─ board context supplied by page

       ├─ therefore no redundant provenance pill

       ├─ subjectless new composer

       ├─ legacy titles still render when present

       └─ Reply → same modal discussion

```



That is substantially simpler than maintaining the current split between a modern Home feed and legacy board pages.



And critically, **the post component, modal, composer, timing, media, excerpts, actions, and eventual Share utility should have one owner.** Home and individual Chatboards become configurations of the same system.



## But this does warrant an audit before another implementation ticket



There are enough legacy behaviors surrounding Chatboards that I do not want us to discover them accidentally while replacing templates.



Codex should inventory the full journey and classify each seam as:



- **reuse unchanged**

- **presentation migration**

- **compatibility bridge required**

- **defer to Community 3.0**

- **retire**



The audit should cover, at minimum:



1. **Routes and entry points** — board indexes, topic URLs, reply URLs, `/chat/`, `/chatboards/`, mentor routes, recent/new-post surfaces, bookmarks and inbound links.

2. **Posting** — current subject-required forms, authentication, board selection, validation, new-topic persistence, post-success behavior.

3. **Reading** — board feed/list, topic page, reply ordering, pagination/depth, media/markup, old titled posts.

4. **Interaction** — Reply, Like, notifications, moderation/reporting, Edit/Delete if present or absent, profile/avatar links.

5. **Board context** — membership, private/public state, board identity, counts, subscriptions/following, board-specific navigation.

6. **Discovery** — Recent Posts, New Posts, search, category/board directories and any SEO/indexable archive behavior.

7. **Commercial/layout dependencies** — ads, rail content, legacy templates, responsive behavior.

8. **Compatibility** — canonical URLs, externally indexed links, historical posts, redirects, anything depended upon outside Community.

9. **Authority boundaries** — which pieces already belong to the adapter/new shared presentation versus legacy page-specific PHP.

10. **Community 3.0 boundary** — avoid spending meaningful effort recreating capabilities that will shortly arrive natively there.



The decisive output should not be code. It should be a **migration map and recommended execution sequence**.



### I would expect the implementation strategy to emerge roughly like this



First establish the shared modern **Chatboard page shell/feed consumer** using the already-proven Home card and modal primitives.



Then migrate one representative board—probably **AI in Education** because we already have good structured fixtures and have examined it repeatedly.



Prove:



> board page → new subjectless composer → persisted post → modern board feed → Reply modal → canonical reply persistence → legacy URL compatibility.



Once that vertical journey passes, migrate the remaining boards largely as **configuration/data**, rather than bespoke page-by-page work.



Only after that would I change the generic directory/navigation entry points to send traffic into the new consumer.



And I would leave canonical historical topic URLs operational through the transition. There is little benefit in immediately breaking indexed URLs merely because users no longer need to navigate to them during normal feed use.

### Blocking is slightly different



I think it's worth investigating now but **not committing to implementation yet**.



“Block user” can mean several things:

5. Suppress notifications involving them.



Those are materially different product/security semantics.



For Teachers.Net v1, the likely useful minimum is:



> **I block User X → their ordinary Community posts/replies disappear from my personal feed/view, and I stop receiving interaction notifications from them where practical.**
